title: Speaker: The Reverse Trick
description: Component lesson. Everything you just learned about microphones, run exactly backwards.

content.value: A microphone turns sound into an electrical signal. A speaker does the exact opposite: it takes an electrical signal and turns it back into sound. ARIA needs this for the ACT half of the loop — telling you something, or giving feedback, instead of only sensing.

A speaker also has a membrane, but this time driven rather than sensed: a changing electrical signal pushes and pulls it back and forth, and that motion pushes the air in front of it, recreating the original pressure wave — sound you can actually hear.

MICROPHONE                          SPEAKER
sound  -->  membrane vibrates       electrical signal --> membrane driven
       -->  electrical signal        -->  air pushed --> sound
(sound to signal)                   (signal to sound — exactly reversed)

content.title: 🔊 Hear it
content.hint: Drag the frequency slider and press Play tone. Notice how the waveform gets denser (more cycles) as the pitch rises.

content.value: How many times the wave repeats per second — its frequency, in Hz — is what your ear perceives as pitch. A low frequency sounds like a low rumble; a high frequency sounds like a high whistle. This is the same "frequency" idea from Module 4's PWM lesson, just applied to something you can actually hear rather than an LED blinking too fast to see.
A buzzer, which you might see on a cheaper robot kit, is really a much simpler cousin of a speaker — usually built to produce one fixed loud tone rather than a controllable range of pitches.
Key takeaway: a speaker is a microphone in reverse — an electrical signal drives a membrane, which pushes air into sound. The signal's frequency directly becomes the pitch you hear.

quiz.question: How is a speaker's job related to a microphone's?
options: A speaker does the exact reverse: electrical signal in, sound out, instead of sound in, signal out
A speaker is just a bigger microphone
quiz.explain: Same membrane idea, opposite direction of conversion — that symmetry is the whole point of this lesson.

quiz.question: What does a signal's frequency become, once it comes out of a speaker as sound?
quiz.explain: How many times per second the wave repeats is exactly what your ear perceives as a high or low pitch.

quiz.question: How does a simple buzzer differ from a full speaker?
options: A buzzer is usually built for one fixed tone, while a speaker can typically produce a controllable range of pitches
There's no real difference at all
Buzzers only work with microphones, not controllers
quiz.explain: A buzzer trades range for simplicity and cost — good enough for a single beep, not for varied tones or speech.
